passage: For decades, ecologists assumed that the tall grasses of the North American prairie survived fire because their growing points sit below the soil, out of the flames' reach. Plant physiologist Alma Reyes argues that this explanation is incomplete. In her plots, grasses that were burned regularly not only survived but grew more vigorously than unburned grasses, apparently because fire cleared away the thick layer of dead stems that otherwise shaded new shoots. Fire, in Reyes's view, is less a threat that prairie grasses withstand than a condition many of them depend on.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Reyes's findings suggest that prairie grasses do not merely tolerate fire but may benefit from it.
Reyes has shown that the growing points of prairie grasses are located deeper than ecologists believed.
Ecologists have long disagreed about whether fire harms or helps the grasses of the prairie.
Unburned prairie grasses grow poorly because they lack the protection that soil provides.
steps: The text sets up an old view (grasses survive fire because growing points are underground) and Reyes's challenge.
Her evidence: regularly burned grasses grew more vigorously, because fire cleared shading dead stems.
The last sentence states the claim: fire is a condition the grasses depend on, not just a threat they withstand.
The other choices misstate her finding, invent a long disagreement, or give the wrong reason unburned grass does worse.
key: The main idea is usually the claim the evidence supports, often restated at the end.
